The project includes asphalt milling and resurfacing, along with roadway repairs in areas affected by tree root intrusions. These improvements are intended to address pavement deterioration, improve roadway conditions, and extend the pavement's useful life. Per the City’s Procurement Code Sec. 2-214(c), City Council approval is required for alternate-source selections, including piggyback purchases exceeding $50,000.00.

The Mobility Plan was adoptedSeptember 16, 2024, and the fees were incorporated into the Land Development Code on May 19, 2025. Councilmember Morgan supported a 90% reduction for long-term single-family residential development and community support services while retaining the base fee and other categories' existing rates. He discussed the effect of large fees on grocery stores, restaurants, medical offices, and other businesses. ITEM 7E – APPROVAL OF AN INCREASE TO THE APPROVED BOUND TREE COOPERATIVE PURCHASING AGREEMENT #24-008PM SPENDING LIMIT FROM $300,000 TO $350,000

Due to the limited time between the two meetings, County staff prepared a revised Agreement that constitutes a complete rewrite of the previous Agreement. In the proposed FY 2026-27 Agreement, funding is limited to $350,000 per year payable to the Flagler Humane Society (FHS) in equal monthly installments of $29,166.67, retroactive to October 1, 2026. Services provided by FHS to the County are divided into Mandatory Services (limited to those required by statute or by code, and including sheltering related to local emergencies) and Additional Services (primarily the sheltering of strays). A section was added by County staff that allows for FHS to request assistance from the Board for any extraordinary circumstances that occur, with the number of animals constituting an extraordinary circumstance changed from five or more animals to 25 or more animals.

As can be expected, the passage of Amendment 3 substantially changes our approach towards this Agreement. County staff contends that this Agreement far exceeds the equivalent share of the funding support provided to FHS by our municipal partners: we continue to fund the bulk of FHS operations through this Agreement. As proposed, Mandatory Services are limited to the required activities and should stay well-below the annual funding provided through this Agreement, while any excess funds (up to the $350,000 annual funding provided) can be used by FHS to provide the Additional Services that are part of the FHS mission and scope, but are not statutory or code requirements for the County to provide or fund. As the County prepares its FY 2027-28 budget, further service level cuts are likely, as well as another shift in the County's approach towards meeting its statutory and code obligations to provide core animal control services.

Analysis Staff is requesting authorization to piggyback Palm Beach County Contract/Project No. 2024050, effective July 2, 2024, through July 1, 2027, awarded to Ranger Construction Industries, Inc. The contract provides established pricing for asphalt milling and resurfacing services, allowing the City to complete the roadway improvements in a cost- effective and efficient manner. Ranger Construction Industries, Inc. provided a quotation in the amount of $234,204.56 for the asphalt refurbishment of Biscayne Drive and Biscayne Boulevard. The proposed work includes milling and resurfacing the existing asphalt pavement, manhole adjustments, and making additional roadway repairs in approximately seven areas affected by tree root intrusions. These locations will require deeper excavation to address the underlying root issues before repairing and resurfacing the roadway. The quotation is based on the pricing established under Palm Beach County’s annual asphalt milling and resurfacing contract.

WHEREAS, City staff recommends that the City Council approve the alternate source selection by piggybacking Palm Beach County Contract/Project No. 2024050 for the asphalt resurfacing and roadway repairs as being in the City’s best. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENACRES, FLORIDA, THAT: SECTION 1. The City Council hereby approves the utilization of Palm Beach County Contract/Project No. 2024050, awarded to Ranger Construction Industries, Inc., for asphalt resurfacing and roadway repairs along Biscayne Drive and Biscayne Boulevard, in an amount not to exceed $234,204.56, in accordance with Section 2-214 of the City’s Code of Ordinances. SECTION 2. The City Council authorizes the appropriate City officials to execute the purchase orders and related documents necessary for these services. SECTION 3. This Resolution shall become effective immediately upon adoption.

Background The City of Greenacres Fire Rescue Department requests approval to purchase twelve (12) sets of firefighter protective turnout gear to replace the temporary stock gear currently issued to existing personnel. Once the new equipment, which is specifically fitted to each firefighter, is received, the existing temporary gear will be retained for future use by firefighters serving their probationary period. This proposed purchase will be made from Municipal Equipment Company, LLC, using Lake County Contract No. 22-730H, Fire Equipment Supplies, and Services, and they have quoted us $50,736.00. Per the City’s Procurement Code Sec. 2-214(c), City Council approval is required for alternate-source selections, including piggyback purchases exceeding $50,000.00.

Analysis Staff is requesting authorization to piggyback Lake County Contract No. 22-730H, Fire Equipment Supplies and Services, effective August 1, 2022, through July 31, 2027, awarded to Municipal Equipment Company, LLC. The contract provides established pricing for fire equipment and supplies, allowing the City to purchase firefighter protective gear cost-effectively and efficiently. Municipal Equipment Company, LLC provided a quotation of $50,736.00 for twelve (12) complete sets of firefighter protective turnout gear. The proposed purchase includes twelve (12) Janesville Super Deluxe protective coats and twelve (12) Janesville Super Deluxe pants with suspenders. The coats are priced at $2,471.00 each, totaling $29,652.00, and the pants are priced at $1,757.00 each, totaling $21,084.00. The quotation also includes freight and is based on the pricing established under Lake County’s Contract.

upcoming.title: BACKGROUND St. Johns Avenue Streetscape Phase II is a downtown infrastructure project supported by City, CRA, and grant funding. The Transfer to Better Place Streetscape II account was included in prior fiscal years’ budget workshops and discussions as a planning allocation for anticipated streetscape improvements. The FY 2025–2026 Central Business District TIF budget included $911,684.00 in this account for transfer to the City’s Better Place Plan Fund. These allocations supported planning discussions but did not identify specific construction costs or establish the CRA’s funding commitment once the project moved into implementation. Staff has not located a CRA resolution or other formal Board action documenting the specific expenditure amounts committed by the CRA. Historically, shared projects such as Streetscape have lacked clear documentation of the City’s and CRA’s respective funding responsibilities and the separate approvals of each governing body. Presenting the proposed CRA expenditures to the CRA Board for approval clarifies the Board’s role in approving CRA funding and creates a public record of the CRA’s contribution.

• Establishes an Exceptional Project Fee, which cannot exceed 200% of the Expedited Permitting Program Fee without approval of the Chief Administrative Officer, for projects based on size, complexity, number of structures or permits, number of required reviewing agencies, phased permitting requirements, or other characteristics requiring greater resources, to be paid in addition to the Expedited Permitting Program Fee
• These fees are supplemental and will not replace, reduce, credit against, or otherwise affect any other fees that are applicable to any project
• The Expedited Permitting Program Fee and Exceptional Project Fee will be deposited as follows: 90% to the Building Inspection Fund and 10% to the Affordable Housing Special Revenue Fund

outgoing_grants.title: Evans Park Renovation – Officially Awarded The City has received an official $1.5 million LWCF grant award for the Evans Park Renovation Project, which ranked 3rd statewide. Evans Park is one of Mount Dora's most popular waterfront destinations for residents and visitors. However, the park currently lacks basic amenities, including public restrooms and supporting infrastructure. These limitations impact everyday park use and require the City to rent equipment or secure sponsorships to provide temporary amenities during special events. The $3 million renovation project will address these longstanding needs through the addition of permanent restrooms, a new outdoor amphitheater, waterfront trail, picnic and gathering areas, and other park improvements. These improvements will enhance the everyday experience for residents while providing the infrastructure needed to better accommodate community events and reduce the City's reliance on temporary facilities.

Award CDBG-DR Funding for San Carlos Island Flood Mitigation Improvements Item Summary: Awards $15,000,000 in Hurricanes Helene and Milton Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) infrastructure funds to the Lee County Department of Transportation for the San Carlos Island Property Acquisition, Flood Mitigation and Resiliency Improvements Project. The project will include parcel acquisition and the reconstruction and improvement of Main Street, including roadway and drainage improvements to enhance the corridor’s safety, functionality, and resilience. The project will serve a predominantly Low- and Moderate-Income (LMI) community and address vulnerabilities identified following Hurricanes Helene and Milton. Board Discussion: Director of Transportation Rob Price presented the item to the Board. Public Comment: The Chairman called for public comment and there were two speakers. Vote: Commissioner Ruane moved approval, seconded by Commissioner Petrosky, called and carried.

Staff recommends motion to approve: an allocation of $2,000,000 of State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program funding for the Flood Disaster Assistance Program (FDAP) to provide financial assistance to eligible homeowners who suffered flood-related damages to homestead properties. Summary: Over November 1 – 2, 2026, Palm Beach County experienced a severe rainfall event resulting in flooding of residential communities and a declared disaster (Fall Flooding) per Executive Order 26-228. The Department of Housing and Economic Development (HED) has identified $2,000,000 in SHIP Program Income which can be made available through the proposed FDAP to offer direct financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners who suffered damages to homestead property caused by the Fall Flooding disaster event. Per SHIP requirements, eligibility will be limited to homeowners with incomes no greater than 140% of Area Median Income (AMI) (currently $179,900 for an eligible household of four [4] persons).

Additionally, the Tallahassee Ethics Code incorporates by reference the statutory definition of “gift.” See § 112.312(12)(a), FLA. STAT. (2026). The statute defines that term, in part, as follows: “Gift,” for purposes of ethics in government and financial disclosure required by law, means that which is accepted by a donee or by another on the donee’s behalf, or that which is paid or given to another for or on behalf of a donee, directly, indirectly, or in trust for the donee’s benefit or by any other means, for which equal or greater consideration is not given within 90 days[.] The City’s prohibition reaches gifts of any value. The relevant question is therefore the character and source of the benefit, rather than whether the amount attributable to an employee falls below a monetary threshold. Due to the limited time between the two meetings, County staff prepared a revised Agreement that constitutes a complete rewrite of the previous Agreement. In the proposed FY 2026-27 Agreement, funding is limited to $350,000 per year payable to the Flagler Humane Society (FHS) in equal monthly installments of $29,166.67, retroactive to October 1, 2026. Services provided by FHS to the County are divided into Mandatory Services (limited to those required by statute or by code, and including sheltering related to local emergencies) and Additional Services (primarily the sheltering of strays). A section was added by County staff that allows for FHS to request assistance from the Board for any extraordinary circumstances that occur, with the number of animals constituting an extraordinary circumstance changed from five or more animals to 25 or more animals.

As can be expected, the passage of Amendment 3 substantially changes our approach towards this Agreement. County staff contends that this Agreement far exceeds the equivalent share of the funding support provided to FHS by our municipal partners: we continue to fund the bulk of FHS operations through this Agreement. As proposed, Mandatory Services are limited to the required activities and should stay well-below the annual funding provided through this Agreement, while any excess funds (up to the $350,000 annual funding provided) can be used by FHS to provide the Additional Services that are part of the FHS mission and scope, but are not statutory or code requirements for the County to provide or fund. As the County prepares its FY 2027-28 budget, further service level cuts are likely, as well as another shift in the County's approach towards meeting its statutory and code obligations to provide core animal control services.

This award will support continuation funding for the Palm Beach County Restore Reentry Program, which provides intensive case management services for individuals released from jail and prison to PBC. The purpose of the project is to reduce recidivism, improve public safety, and address barriers to successful reintegration during the critical post release period. Over the past three (3) years, the Palm Beach County Restore Reentry Program has served 1,247 adults returning from incarceration. City of Tallahassee Independent Ethics Board AO 2026-08 – November 17, 2026 Page 5 of 6 The Board previously recognized this distinction in AO 2023-01, at 6 n.2. 1 These authorities support treating a contribution as a gift to the City when the City receives and independently administers it for an authorized City purpose. They do not establish a blanket exception for benefits merely routed through a City account. The City must exercise actual control, and the arrangement must not serve as a means for a vendor to provide an indirect gift to a covered individual. Additionally, the Florida Commission previously provided guidance to the City of Tallahassee on a similar matter. The Commission concluded that event tickets purchased by the City as part of a sponsorship package and subsequently distributed to officials and employees were gifts to the officials and employees from the City. By contrast, complimentary tickets supplied by outside organizations to officials and employees but distributed through the City for their benefit were indirect gifts from the outside organizations. The ARB voted unanimously to recommend that the Collins House be placed on the Local Register of Historic Places and be rezoned to include an HPO.

Background: The Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program (IRLNEP) opened their request for proposals on October 15, 2026, for grant funding opportunities for the October 1, 2027, through September 30, 2028, fiscal year. The current IRLNEP request allows for proposal submittals in multiple Indian River Lagoon benefiting categories; Water Quality Restoration Projects, Habitat Restoration Projects, Community Based Restoration Projects and Science and Innovation Projects. Proposals must be submitted by December 14, 2026, to be eligible for the review and ranking. Staff is requesting Board of County Commissioner (BOCC) approval to submit relevant proposals under this funding opportunity.

Should a County proposal be accepted for an award of funding from the IRLNEP, staff from the respective Department will bring the recommended award of funding to the BOCC for consideration and acceptance.

Staff Recommendation: Staff recommends the Board of County Commissioners authorize the submittal of proposals for the Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program's 2028 funding cycle. If awarded, staff will bring any grant award contracts back to the BOCC for acceptance and execution.

SUMMARY: On March 10, 2026, the Village adopted an ordinance annexing approximately 446.14 acres of land, known as Artistry Lakes. The County objected to the annexation because the annexation area does not meet the requirements of Section 171.043, Florida Statutes. On March 26, 2026, the County passed a resolution initiating the Conflict Resolution Procedures under Chapter 164. Florida Statutes. On February 10, 2026, after discussions with the County, the Village initiated the Interlocal Service Boundary Agreement (ISBA) process to negotiate the terms under which the subject property and adjacent properties will be annexed. The County adopted its responding resolution on February 26, 2026. While the Village approved the ISBA, the Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners (BCC) denied it on August 26, 2026. On September 30th, 2026 the County Administrator and the Village Manager met per Ch. 164 Conflict Resolution Proceedings. Both the County Administrator and the Village Manager agreed to bring the ILA to their respective governing bodies. The County also agreed to bring the PBA to the BCC at the same time as the ILA. The Village Council approved the ILA on October 13, 2026.

2026 Congestion Management Process | 1-1 1 Introduction The Congestion Management Process (CMP) is a data-driven, detailed, and systematic process conducted by the Collier Metropolitan Planning Organization (MPO) to provide for the safe and effective management and operation of new and existing transportation facilities by using travel demand reduction and operational management strategies. The MPO is required by the federal government to implement a CMP as part of its routine planning efforts. Having a functional CMP that results in low-cost improvements or strategies benefits the regional transportation system by providing a defined approach for the MPO to address congestion concerns linked to transportation, livability, and land use. Projects identified through the CMP are coordinated with the MPO’s Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP) in terms of identifying future revenue commitments and establishing planning consistency. 1.1 Federal Guidance The initial federal requirements for congestion management were introduced by the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act (ISTEA) of 1991 and were continued under its successor, the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century

One of the funding methods available for capital improvements and essential services is to create the Municipal Service Benefit Unit (MSBU) and levy non-ad valorem special assessments on those properties that derive a direct benefit from the improvements. This type of assessment is based on benefit and collected along with property taxes using the uniform method pursuant to Section 197.3632 of the Florida Statutes. In order to preserve this funding option, it is necessary for the Board to adopt a resolution expressing its intent to use the uniform method of collecting commencing in November 2027. The resolutions must be considered at a duly advertised public hearing held prior to January 1, 2027. The MSBU process is typically started when a majority of property owners submit petitions to the County requesting that an MSBU be created. The mentioned resolutions do not in any way obligate the County to levy special assessments; rather, they simply satisfy the legal requirement, preserving the County's option to use a uniform method of collection if special assessments are levied. Requests for grants of General Fund ad valorem taxes may be accepted from eligible municipal organizations that plan to invest in Public Facilities within the County and shall not exceed $50,000 within a fiscal year. The term “Public Facilities” means capital improvements that have a life expectancy of five or more years, which meet a public purpose and will be available for use by the general public. On October 27, 2025, the Board approved the City of Fernandina Beach’s request for Municipal Grant Funding for the Martin Luther King Jr. Sports Fields redevelopment, in the amount of $50,000. It stands as a prime example of a successful working waterfront that serves both economic and recreational needs. WHERE Sparkman Wharf is located on the site of the formerly under performing Channelside Bay Plaza, part of the Water Street Tampa project. It sits along the Garrison Channel in downtown Tampa. WHAT Sparkman Wharf revitalizes a previously underutilized waterfront area, combining a working port with retail, dining, and entertainment options. The project is named after Stephen Sparkman, Tampa’s first congressman, known for his efforts in securing federal funding for Port Tampa Bay. Developed through a partnership between Tampa Bay Lightning owner Jeff Vinik and Bill Gates’ Cascade Investment, Sparkman Wharf replaced the failed Channelside Bay Plaza. The development includes a one-acre event lawn, a biergarten, a dining garden, and waterfront loft-style office spaces. Year-round programming of live music and events accommodates up to 500 people

To: Historic Preservation Board From: Kyle Wilkes, Senior Planner Date: November 10, 2026 Re: Certificate of Appropriateness COA-26-0001 - Construction of a Church Thrift Store At 317 S Mary Street (Ak 1189799) Introduction: The St. Thomas Episcopal Church currently operates a church ministry thrift store at 211 S Mary Street. The church has entered into an agreement with the Lake County School Board to grant the church-owned land to Eustis Elementary. The School Board's planned campus improvements, which include both this property and the main campus, will require demolishing or relocating the existing building that contains the thrift store. St. Thomas is requesting a Certificate of Appropriateness to construct a new building to house the thrift store. The applicant has provided anticipated floor plans and sketch elevations. This COA requests only the Historic Preservation Board's approval for the new thrift store construction, as the existing thrift store at 211 S Mary Street is outside the Washington Avenue Historic District.

The CMP Strategy Evaluation Criteria (see Appendix G) are used to evaluate project submittals for consistency with CMP Goals, Objectives, strategy toolbox, and hot spot congestion corridors. Projects developed consistent with the CMP Strategy Toolbox are submitted for funding consideration and evaluated by the CMC using the Strategy Evaluation Criteria. Based on this evaluation, the CMC provides recommendations to the MPO Board for project prioritization within the Transportation Improvement Program (TIP), consistent with the MPO’s most recent Long Range Transportation Plan (2050 LRTP). CMP projects that advance into project development and programming are typically funded with the Federal Surface Transportation Block Grant funds that are allocated to the Urbanized Area, consistent with the 2050 LRTP Cost Feasible Plan. These funds will be used to partially fund the Josh Lee Boulevard Complete Streets Capital Improvement Project, which includes significant work along Josh Lee Boulevard, adjacent to the City's new parking garage.

Funds disbursed by FTA can only be distributed to a direct recipient and there are limited entities that qualify as a direct recipient. To address this issue, the City would like to enter into an agreement with the Broward Metropolitan Planning Organization (BMPO) for them to be our direct recipient of the funds. The City already has an Interlocal Agreement with the Broward Metropolitan Planning Organization (BMPO), to administer the grant award funds on the City’s behalf, which was approved by the City Commission on December 12 th , 2023. To continue the process with the BMPO to be able to receive the FTA funds, a Subrecipient Agreement between the City of Sunrise and BMPO is necessary. The Subrecipient Agreement includes funding for the BMPO expenses up to $250,000 of the Grant for BMPO’s administration and oversight and $2,250,000 (“Grant Funds”) to reimburse the City for design and construction of improvements for the Project.

79. Public Information and Education Items. Public Information and Education Items are defined as materials whose purpose is to convey substantive information about highway safety. Paper, pamphlets, flash drives, CD-ROMs, and similar media that contain educational materials are all allowable because their purpose is to contain and convey educational information. In order to be considered educational, distributed material must provide substantial informational and educational content to the public (not merely a slogan) and have the sole purpose of conveying that information. If a Subrecipient chooses to provide educational content on a flash drive, CD-ROM, or similar device, that device must be an economical method of conveying the information. Before printing or ordering any public information and education items, a final draft or drawing of the items shall be submitted to the FDOT State Safety Office for review and approval. Requests should include the following: (a) What public information or educational item is being requested (b) What program/policy is the item supporting (c) Who the target audience is (d) How the item will be distributed (e) Estimated unit cost(s) for the item

At Broward College, we witness firsthand the life-changing impact of the School Readiness program. For many of our student-parents, access to affordable, high-quality childcare is not merely a support service, it is the deciding factor in whether they can persist, complete their degrees, and transition successfully into the workforce. By alleviating this critical financial burden, ELC Broward empowers parents with stability and peace of mind, enabling them to fully invest in their education and career advancement. The City of Sunrise’s investment in this initiative yields far-reaching benefits beyond individual families. It strengthens the local economy by supporting small childcare businesses and sustaining the educators who serve our youngest learners. At the same time, it ensures that children enter school socially and academically prepared laying the foundation for long-term success that benefits the entire community. The Third Amendment to the ILA was developed in collaboration between Broward County and the Broward County City Manager’s Association (BCCMA). It included reprioritization of the current distribution of Transportation Surtax funding to Municipalities among Community Shuttle, Capital Projects, and Rehabilitation and Maintenance (R&M) Projects; a creation of a new Formula-based Funding model for R&M Projects and On-Demand Transportation during County Fiscal Years 2026 to 2032, subject to availability of Transportation Surtax funding; the development of a new means of allowing Municipalities the ability to obtain Transportation Surtax funding to be used as required local match in relation to state and federal appropriations and grants; provided Municipalities with flexibility on how each will use Formula-based Funding from the Transportation Surtax; and outlined the criteria for evaluating process, documented the allocation for municipal capital projects, and included other minor changes.

One of the City Commission programs that has been proposed is a "Blue Tarp" Roof Repair and Replacement Program (Program) for homesteaded single-family homes located east of Pine Island Road. It is the intent of this Program to target roof assembly repairs and roof assembly replacements for existing residential homes with "Blue Tarps." For the purpose of this Program, "Blue Tarp" is defined as any type of waterproof general-purpose tarp, of any color, that has been temporarily fastened to a damaged roof to prevent water intrusion. Analysis Staff is requesting authorization to piggyback Palm Beach County Contract/Project No. 2024050, effective July 2, 2024, through July 1, 2027, awarded to Ranger Construction Industries, Inc. The contract provides established pricing for asphalt milling and resurfacing services, allowing the City to complete the roadway improvements in a cost- effective and efficient manner. Ranger Construction Industries, Inc. provided a quotation in the amount of $234,204.56 for the asphalt refurbishment of Biscayne Drive and Biscayne Boulevard. The proposed work includes milling and resurfacing the existing asphalt pavement, manhole adjustments, and making additional roadway repairs in approximately seven areas affected by tree root intrusions. These locations will require deeper excavation to address the underlying root issues before repairing and resurfacing the roadway. The quotation is based on the pricing established under Palm Beach County’s annual asphalt milling and resurfacing contract.

WHEREAS, City staff recommends that the City Council approve the alternate source selection by piggybacking Palm Beach County Contract/Project No. 2024050 for the asphalt resurfacing and roadway repairs as being in the City’s best. 16. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. The parties shall cooperate to resolve any dispute pertaining to this Cooperative Purchasing Master Agreement efficiently, as timely as practicable, and at the lowest possible level with authority to resolve such dispute. If, however, a dispute persists and cannot be resolved, it may be escalated within each organization. In such situation, upon notice by either party, each party, within five (5) business days shall reduce its description of the dispute to writing and deliver it to the other party. The receiving party then shall have three (3) business days to review and respond in writing. In the event that the parties cannot then agree on a resolution of the dispute, the parties shall schedule a conference between the respective senior managers of each organization to attempt to resolve the dispute. In the event the parties cannot agree, either party may resort to court to resolve the dispute.

Description ATY Resolution - C26165 Proposal and Appendix Sole Source Sunbiz - Hoover Pumping Systems Corporation Background: The Bridges at Springtree Golf Club is a 67-acre, par 62 executive golf course, which first opened in 1972. Since that time it has undergone significant renovatio ns; however, the existing irrigation pump station has been in continuous operation for 25 years. It has now reach the end of its useful life as many of its critical components are outdated and beyond their typical 15-20 year lifespan. The irrigation pump station is a critical component of the golf course and as such, it is necessary to maintain it in peak condition to ensure business continuity and optimal operating condition year round to avoid any potential disruptions. The Bridges at Springtree Golf Club is extremely busy and remains in high demand among many City residents and visitors.

In addition to the state-administered opioid funds, Indian River County occasionally has an opportunity to receive direct distribution of opioid settlement monies. Recently, the County Attorney's office learned of a new national opioid settlement with Albertsons grocery/pharmacy. The Albertsons national settlement totals $774 million and it resolves claims that the grocery and pharmacy improperly dispensed prescription painkillers and failed to prevent opioid misuse. The settlement funds are being distributed to states, local governments, and tribes. In order to participate, the Board must approve the attached Subdivision Participation and Release Form. Although the amount that the County will receive is unclear, the funds will come directly to the County and will be distributed to the 19th Judicial Circuit Drug Court programs and used for assessment, treatment, testing and wrap-around services, such as housing and transportation.

The event will attract up to 120 athletes, generate 400 room nights, and attract over 300 spectators for the event. Staff recommends funding up to $7,500 for this event. This support will help offset costs associated with venue rentals and other logistics, ensuring the success of the event. The CVB uses the Destinations International Economic Impact Calculator, used by over 300 destination organizations for all events, to ensure consistent reporting. For this event, the Calculator estimates an Economic Impact of $585,000. Staff utilizes the Board-approved Athletic Event & Tournament Application to evaluate whether the organization qualifies for funding. In making this determination, several key factors are considered, including the seasonality of the event, its potential for future iterations, projected economic impact through direct spending and bed tax revenue, and the level of marketing value. NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the City Council of the City of St. Petersburg, Florida, that (I) the Community Development Block Grant -Disaster Recovery Agreement between the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”), Pinellas County, Florida (“County”) and the City of St. Petersburg, Florida (“ City”) related to a geo-coding error that resulted in $173,681,000 in CDBG-DR funds that should have been part of the City’s federal award being included in the County’s federal award (“Misallocated Funds”) and (ii) the CDBG -DR Funds Coordination Agreement between the County and the City that establishes a coordinated and efficient framework for the use and oversight of the misallocated funds are hereby approved.

EXPLANATION: Congress appropriated funds through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) Program in response to the 2023 Hurricane Idalia (DR-4734-FL) and the 2024 Hurricane Helene (DR-4828- FL). Assistance for these disasters was appropriated on December 21, 2024, by the Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2025. The City of St. Petersburg (City) was allocated $159,884,000 per the Allocation Announcement Notice (90 FR 4759) published on January 16, 2025. On June 12, 2025, City Council approved the CDBG-DR Action Plan for the use of the federal grant funds (Resolution No. 2025-327) which allocated $6,000,000 to the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program. HUD approved the City’s Action Plan in August 2025 and executed the City’s Grant Agreement in February 2026. Through extensive public input and Unmet Needs and Mitigation Needs Assessments in the Action Plan, the City determined the need to create the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program to address the increased need for essential community services as a result of the qualifying disasters. Re: Resolution Number 2026-113: Assignment of Commercial Contract and Addendum and Associated Budget Amendment Introduction: The City has an opportunity to acquire 44 Sharps Circle through assignment of the Commercial Contract and First Addendum between Hometown Property Investments, LLC (Assignor) and Lake Eustis MHP, LLC (Seller). The acquisition is subject to existing lawful tenancies, with any later closure, relocation or demolition requiring separate implementation under applicable law. Background: The subject property has been identified as a catalyst site in the Downtown Master Plan and is key to the future execution of that plan. The parcels are identified by the Lake County Property Appraiser as: • 11-19-26-0200-061-00000 and, • 11-19-26-0200-068-00000 The City has attempted to acquire these parcels historically and they are instrumental to the success of the waterfront activation component of the Downtown Master Plan. Statutory Requirements: The acquisition will proceed under Section 2-404 of the Eustis Code without using the public records exemption in Section 166.045, Florida Statutes. Two MAI appraisals are required before purchase. If the price exceeds their average, approval requires four affirmative votes at a public hearing with an opportunity for public input. Any necessary budget amendment will be adopted by resolution under Section 2-193 of the Code. Legal/Policy Analysis: The City Attorney has reviewed the proposed transaction which provides for: • Termination at the City’s sole discretion during the remaining Due Diligence Period by timely written notice. • Title and survey review and environmental inspections under the Contract and First Addendum. • Commission approval and Finance confirmation of appropriated funds available when due before City execution. • City Attorney written authorization before disbursement of the City’s closing funds. Upon effectiveness of the Assignment and Seller’s Consent, the City will assume Buyer’s rights, obligations, and liabilities under the Contract. The Agreement imposes no undue obligations and reflects standard municipal acquisition protections.

Sta ff presented Phase Two of the Well No. 3 project, which was identified in the City’s master plan to improve water system reliability and accommodate future growth. Staff reported that the well had been drilled to approximately 650 feet and that Phase Two would include the electrical work, piping, and other improvements needed to place it into service. Sta ff explained that the additional well would help maintain water service and adequate fire flow if Water Treatment Plant No. 1 were out of service or undergoing maintenance. Staff also discussed plans for a second storage tank to increase capacity and pr ovide backup storage. The Phase Two cost, including contingency, was just under $1 million, compared with the engineer’s estimate of approximately $1.5 million. In re sponse to a Council question, staff confirmed that Well No. 3 was drilled to approximately the same depth as most of the City’s other wells. Staff noted that deeper drilling would substantially increase costs and make it more difficult to manage sand drawn through the limestone. Mayor Homich opened public comment. No one spoke. Study Findings The study's primary objective was to provide the City's decision makers with the basic data needed to make informed pricing decisions. This report details the full cost of each service for which a fee is charged and presents proposed fees and fiscal projections based on recommended cost recovery levels. The fee analysis adheres to Florida State Law which is based on the "estimated reasonable cost of providing a service". It is MGT’s recommendation that, in years where a detailed fee study is not undertaken, fees should be adjusted to reflect changes in City staffing, expenditures or service offerings. Approve Contract Change Order for Lynn Hall Restroom and Site Improvements Item Summary: Approves a change order to the contract with Wright Construction Group for additional constructional services in the amount of $547,542.52, bringing the new contract total to $6,692,910.20. This portion of the project will be funded by FDEM LAP Fund, Bed Taxes through the Beach and Shoreline Program, and Regional Park Impact Fees. This change order includes additional pile removal work and revisions to the project scope resulting from unforeseen conditions and permitting reviews. During demolition, the existing piles were found to be approximately 25 feet deep rather than the 14 feet shown in the existing structural drawings, which required larger equipment to remove them. Also, revisions include changes to site and building lighting, sea turtle barriers, construction fencing, door hardware and interior finishes, colored concrete at the memorial star, and storm drainage modifications to meet permit requirements.

Background: The Capital Improvements Element (CIE) of the Highlands County 2050 Comprehensive Plan considers the County’s need for and location of public facilities and infrastructure. The CIE establishes policies to ensure that adequate public facilities are available to meet established acceptable levels of service (LOS) for existing and future development , consistent with the requirements of Section 163.3177(3)(a), Florida Statutes. This includes consideration of the impacts of new development on facilities such as roads, parks and recreation, drainage, water and wastewater systems, and schools.
